questions.question: Compared with a batch job, which reads a bounded input, what can a stream processor do that the batch job structurally cannot?

options.text: Emit results per event as it arrives, not after the input ends
Make each input record affect the output exactly once despite task failures
Join two separate datasets on a key that both of them share
Partition its input so that many machines work on it in parallel

questions.explanation: A batch job assumes bounded input: it knows when it has read everything, and an operation such as sorting cannot emit anything until the last record is seen, because that record might sort first. A stream is unbounded, so a stream processor handles each event incrementally as it arrives and updates its output continuously. The other abilities are not unique to streams: batch frameworks already give effectively-once output by retrying failed tasks and discarding partial output, they join datasets by key, and they partition work across many machines.

questions.question: What key assumption about its input does batch processing (for example, a MapReduce job) rely on?

options.text: That the input is bounded, of a known and finite size
That the input fits into the memory of a single machine
That the input has already been sorted by key beforehand
That the input arrives in order of its event timestamps

questions.explanation: A batch job assumes bounded input, so it knows when it has finished reading. Sorting, central to MapReduce, depends on this: the very last input record could have the lowest key and need to be output first, so output cannot start until all input is read. Batch jobs do not need input to fit in memory (MapReduce sorts on disk), do not need pre-sorted input (the framework sorts it), and do not depend on arrival order because they read embedded timestamps.

questions.question: Why is a dataset of user activity never 'complete' in any meaningful sense, forcing batch systems to cut it into chunks such as one day of data?

options.text: Users keep producing new data, so the input is unbounded
The dataset is too large for any single job to read in full
Databases delete old records before a batch job can read them
Records at the edges of each chunk are routinely corrupted

questions.explanation: Much real data arrives gradually: users produced data yesterday and today and will produce more tomorrow, so unless the business stops, the dataset keeps growing. Batch processors therefore artificially divide it into fixed-duration chunks, such as processing each day's data at the end of the day. Size is not the issue, since distributed batch jobs read huge datasets in full; the issue is that the dataset never stops growing.

questions.question: What problem with daily batch jobs motivates stream processing?

options.text: Input changes reach the derived output only about a day later
A daily job must hold the whole day's input in memory before it starts
A failed daily job cannot be retried without losing that day's input
A daily job cannot read input written by more than one producer

questions.explanation: With a daily batch, a change in the input appears in the output up to a day later, which is too slow for many users. Running the batch more often (every hour, every second) reduces the delay; stream processing goes further, abandoning fixed time slices and processing every event as it happens. The distractors are false for batch jobs: they spill to disk rather than needing everything in memory, they can be retried because their input is immutable, and they read input from any number of producers.

questions.question: A stream is data made incrementally available over time. In which familiar technologies does this general idea already appear? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Audio and video delivered over the internet
Unix stdin and stdout, and lazy lists in programming languages
File input-stream APIs such as Java's FileInputStream, and TCP connections
A batch job that starts only once its fixed input file is completely written

questions.explanation: A stream is any sequence of data made available bit by bit over time, so a consumer can act on early parts before later parts exist. Streaming media, Unix pipes, lazy lists, file input streams, and TCP connections all work this way. A batch job that waits for a finished, fixed-size file is the opposite: it processes bounded, already-complete input.

optionExplanations.a: Audio and video arrive as successive chunks that can be played before the whole media file exists. Incremental availability, not the content type, is what makes them streams.
optionExplanations.b: Unix pipes deliver bytes as the upstream process produces them, and lazy lists compute elements on demand. Both let a consumer act before a complete collection exists.
optionExplanations.c: FileInputStream yields a file's bytes incrementally, and TCP delivers an ordered byte sequence over time. Neither requires the caller to receive one completed value first.
optionExplanations.d: Waiting until a fixed input file is completely written is bounded batch processing, not streaming. The job cannot start until the whole input exists, which is exactly what a stream avoids.

questions.question: In stream processing, what is an event?

options.text: A small, self-contained, immutable object recording something that happened
A mutable record that is updated in place as circumstances change over time
A batch of records grouped together by the time window they fall into
An acknowledgment message sent back to the broker by a consumer

questions.explanation: An event is the streaming equivalent of a record: a small, self-contained, immutable object describing something that happened at some point in time, usually with a time-of-day timestamp. Examples are a user viewing a page or making a purchase, a temperature reading, a CPU metric, or one line of a web server log. It is immutable because it records a past fact; a later change is a new event, not an edit of the old one. A window groups many events, and an acknowledgment is a control message, not the data itself.

questions.question: Once an event has been encoded (as text, JSON, or a binary format), what does the encoding make possible?

options.text: Storing it (say, appending to a file) and sending it to another node
Storing it durably, though sending it needs a separate network encoding
Sending it to another node, though storing it needs conversion to a table row
Processing it only inside the program that encoded it, in the same process

questions.explanation: Encoding turns an event into bytes, and the same bytes serve both purposes: they can be stored (appended to a file, inserted into a relational table, or written to a document database) and sent over the network to another node for processing. No second encoding is needed for either purpose. Being able to move and persist events independently of the producing process is what lets several consumers process the same events.

questions.question: In a streaming system, which roles generate and process events, and what groups related events together (as a filename groups related records in a filesystem)?

options.text: Producers generate events, consumers process them, and a topic groups them
Writers generate events, readers process them, and an offset groups them
Leaders generate events, followers process them, and a segment groups them
Coordinators generate events, participants process them, and a directory groups them

questions.explanation: An event is generated once by a producer (also called a publisher or sender) and may be processed by several consumers (subscribers or recipients). Related events are grouped into a topic or stream, which plays the role a filename plays for a set of related records in batch processing. An offset is a position inside a partition, a segment is a chunk of a log file on disk, and leader/follower and coordinator/participant are replication and two-phase-commit roles, not event roles.

questions.question: In principle a producer could write events to a file or database and consumers could poll it for new ones. Why is this a poor fit for continual, low-delay processing?

options.text: Frequent polls mostly find nothing new, so overhead rises as the delay shrinks
A database cannot store events, because events are immutable and rows are not
A file cannot be appended to while another process is reading from it
Polling cannot work across a network, so consumers must run on the database host

questions.explanation: Polling works for daily batches, but the more often you poll to reduce delay, the smaller the fraction of requests that return new events, so overhead grows. It is better for consumers to be notified when events appear. Databases have traditionally supported notification poorly: triggers can react to an inserted row, but they are limited and were somewhat of an afterthought, so specialized event-delivery tools were built. Files and databases can store events and be appended to while being read; the problem is the cost of polling.

questions.question: How does a publish/subscribe messaging system extend a direct channel such as a Unix pipe or a TCP connection?

options.text: It lets many producers send to one topic and many consumers receive from it
It adds durable storage, but still links exactly one sender to one recipient
It replaces push delivery with consumers polling a shared file for messages
It adds nothing structural, since a pipe already links many senders to many recipients

questions.explanation: A Unix pipe or TCP connection links exactly one sender to one recipient. A messaging system lets multiple producer nodes send messages to the same topic and multiple consumer nodes receive messages from it, with messages pushed to consumers. Durability varies between messaging systems and is not the defining addition, and messaging systems exist precisely to avoid consumers polling a datastore.

questions.question: Within the publish/subscribe model, which two questions are most useful for telling messaging systems apart? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: What happens if the producers send messages faster than the consumers can process them?
What happens if nodes crash or temporarily go offline — are any messages lost?
What query language does the messaging system expose to its consumers?
How many partitions may a single topic be divided into at most?

questions.explanation: Messaging systems take many approaches and none is right for every purpose. Two questions separate them: what happens when producers send faster than consumers can process (drop, buffer in a queue, or apply backpressure), and what happens when nodes crash or go offline (are messages lost, which depends on disk writes and replication). Query languages and partition limits are product details that do not determine overload or failure behavior.

optionExplanations.a: When production exceeds consumption, a system must drop messages, buffer them, or apply backpressure. That policy determines overload behavior and resource needs.
optionExplanations.b: Crash handling determines whether messages survive producer, broker, or consumer outages. Durability needs disk writes and/or replication, which cost throughput and latency.
optionExplanations.c: Brokers usually let consumers subscribe to topics or patterns rather than run arbitrary queries. A query language does not define how the system behaves under overload or failure.
optionExplanations.d: Partition-count limits are product-specific capacity details, not a semantic distinction. Systems with very different limits can behave identically under overload and crashes.

questions.question: In a messaging system, what are the three broad options when producers send messages faster than consumers can process them?

options.text: Drop messages, buffer them in a queue, or apply backpressure
Drop the message, retry sending it later, or abort the producer process
Buffer, compress, or partition the message stream across more brokers
Replicate, shard, or cache the pending messages

questions.explanation: The system can drop messages, buffer them in a queue, or apply backpressure (flow control), which blocks the producer from sending more. Unix pipes and TCP use backpressure: a small fixed-size buffer that, when full, blocks the sender until the recipient takes data out. With buffering, the key question is what happens as the queue grows: does the system crash when the queue no longer fits in memory, or spill to disk, and how much does disk access slow it down? Retrying, compressing, partitioning, or caching do not resolve a sustained rate mismatch on their own.

questions.question: In a messaging system, what does guaranteeing that messages survive crashes typically cost, and what can you gain if occasional loss is acceptable?

options.text: Disk writes and/or replication; accepting loss can raise throughput and cut latency
Only extra disk space; accepting loss saves space but not throughput or latency
Only extra latency; accepting loss lowers latency but also lowers throughput
Only consumer acknowledgments; accepting loss removes those and changes nothing else

questions.explanation: As with databases, durability requires writing to disk, replicating, or both, and that has a cost. If you can afford to lose messages sometimes, you can usually get higher throughput and lower latency on the same hardware. Whether loss is acceptable depends on the application: an occasional missing periodic sensor reading may not matter because a fresh value arrives soon, but if you are counting events, every lost message makes the counters wrong.

questions.question: What strong reliability guarantee do batch processing frameworks such as MapReduce provide?

options.text: Failed tasks are retried and their partial output is discarded
Tasks never fail at all, because the input files are immutable
Every task runs exactly once, so retries are never needed
All output is replicated to three machines before the job ends

questions.explanation: Batch frameworks automatically retry failed tasks and automatically discard their partial output, so the job's output is the same as if no failures had occurred. This makes programming simpler. Tasks do fail, and they may run more than once; immutability of the input is what makes rerunning them safe, not what prevents failure. Getting a similar guarantee is a central goal of stream-processing fault tolerance.

questions.question: Which of these accurately describe direct producer-to-consumer messaging that works without an intermediary broker? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: UDP multicast for low-latency financial feeds, with application-level retransmission of lost packets
Brokerless libraries such as ZeroMQ and nanomsg, doing publish/subscribe over TCP or IP multicast
StatsD and Brubeck sending metrics over unreliable UDP, so their counters are at best approximate
Webhooks, which guarantee delivery because the caller retries until the receiver acknowledges

questions.explanation: Direct messaging sends from producer to consumer with no broker in between: UDP multicast for stock-market feeds, brokerless libraries such as ZeroMQ and nanomsg, UDP metrics collectors such as StatsD and Brubeck, and webhooks, where a service calls a registered callback URL. These work well in their niches, but the application must be aware of possible message loss: they generally assume producers and consumers are always online. A consumer that is offline misses messages, and producer retries fail if the producer crashes and loses its buffer of messages to retry.

optionExplanations.a: UDP multicast sends directly from the producer to receivers with no broker, favoring low latency. Reliability is added above UDP: the producer remembers sent packets and retransmits on request.
optionExplanations.b: ZeroMQ and nanomsg provide brokerless publish/subscribe over TCP or multicast. No durable intermediary holds messages, so the application owns availability and recovery.
optionExplanations.c: StatsD and Brubeck emit metrics over unreliable UDP without a broker. Because StatsD counters are correct only if every message arrives, losses make them approximate.
optionExplanations.d: Webhooks are direct, but retries do not guarantee delivery: the calling service may crash and lose the messages it meant to retry, or the receiver may stay offline.

questions.question: What is a message broker (also called a message queue)?

options.text: A server between producers and consumers, essentially a database for message streams
A stateless router that forwards each message immediately to consumers and stores nothing
A client library linked into producers that sends messages straight to consumers
A protocol that blocks every producer whenever any consumer is slower than it

questions.explanation: A message broker is essentially a kind of database optimized for handling message streams. It runs as a server; producers write messages to it and consumers read from it as clients. Centralizing the data lets the system tolerate clients that connect, disconnect, and crash, and moves the durability question to the broker (some keep messages in memory only, others write to disk). Faced with slow consumers, brokers generally queue without limit rather than drop messages or apply backpressure. Consumers are therefore asynchronous: a producer waits only for the broker to confirm it buffered the message, not for consumers to process it.

questions.question: Which of these are real differences between traditional (JMS/AMQP-style) message brokers and databases? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Most brokers delete a message once it has been delivered, so they suit long-term storage poorly
Brokers assume a small working set; a large backlog spilling to disk can degrade throughput
Databases offer secondary indexes and search; brokers offer subscription to topics by pattern
Like a database query, a broker returns a point-in-time snapshot and never notifies clients

questions.explanation: Brokers and databases have converged somewhat (some brokers even take part in two-phase commit via XA or JTA), but practical differences remain. Databases keep data until it is explicitly deleted, while most brokers delete messages after delivery. Brokers assume short queues and slow down when a backlog builds. Databases select data through indexes and queries, brokers through topic subscriptions. And a database query returns a snapshot that silently goes stale, while a broker notifies clients when new data arrives. This traditional view is embodied in JMS and AMQP and products such as RabbitMQ, ActiveMQ, and IBM MQ.

optionExplanations.a: Traditional brokers delete messages once delivered, whereas databases keep records until explicitly deleted. A delete-on-delivery queue is therefore a poor long-term store of history.
optionExplanations.b: A broker designed for short transient queues can slow sharply when consumers lag and the backlog spills to disk, because each message then takes longer to process.
optionExplanations.c: Databases select records with secondary indexes and queries, while brokers let clients subscribe to topics matching a pattern. Both pick the data a client cares about, by different mechanisms.
optionExplanations.d: This reverses the real difference: a database query returns a point-in-time snapshot that can go stale silently, whereas a broker notifies clients when new messages arrive.

questions.question: When several consumers read messages from the same topic, how do the load-balancing and fan-out patterns differ?

options.text: Load balancing gives each message to one consumer; fan-out gives each message to all
Load balancing gives each message to all consumers; fan-out gives each message to one
Both give every message to every consumer, differing only in delivery order
Both give each message to one consumer, differing only in how it is chosen

questions.explanation: With load balancing, each message goes to one of the consumers, so they share the work; it suits messages that are expensive to process (in AMQP, several clients consume from one queue; in JMS this is a shared subscription). With fan-out, each message goes to every consumer, so independent consumers can each tune in to the same broadcast, like several batch jobs reading one input file (JMS topic subscriptions, AMQP exchange bindings). The two combine: several consumer groups each receive every message, while within a group only one node receives each message.

questions.question: Why do message brokers require consumers to acknowledge messages?

options.text: A consumer may crash mid-processing, so messages are removed only once processed
They provide flow control only, and the broker never redelivers a message
They guarantee that messages are processed in exactly the order the producer sent them
They only report consumer throughput to operators and do not affect delivery

questions.explanation: A broker may deliver a message to a consumer that crashes before finishing it. With acknowledgments, the client explicitly tells the broker when it has finished processing, and only then does the broker remove the message. If the connection closes or times out without an acknowledgment, the broker assumes the message was not processed and delivers it to another consumer. This prevents loss but can cause duplicates: if processing finished and only the acknowledgment was lost, the message is processed twice, which only an atomic commit protocol can rule out. Redelivery also tends to reorder messages rather than preserve order.

questions.question: A broker load-balances messages m1 to m5 from one producer across consumers 1 and 2, using acknowledgments. Consumer 2 crashes while processing m3, while consumer 1 is processing m4. The broker redelivers the unacknowledged m3 to consumer 1. In what order does consumer 1 process m3, m4, and m5?

options.text: m4, then m3, then m5, so m3 and m4 run out of send order
m3, then m4, then m5, because the broker preserves send order
m4, then m5; m3 is lost because it was never acknowledged
m3, then m4, then m5, with m4 processed a second time

questions.explanation: Consumer 1 is already busy with m4 when m3 is redelivered, so it processes m4, then the redelivered m3, then m5. m3 and m4 are thus processed in a different order from the one the producer sent them in. Even if the broker otherwise tries to preserve order (as JMS and AMQP require), combining load balancing with redelivery inevitably reorders messages. m3 is not lost, because the missing acknowledgment is what triggers redelivery. To avoid reordering, use a separate queue per consumer; reordering matters only if messages have causal dependencies.

questions.question: In an AMQP/JMS-style broker, what happens to a message after the consumer acknowledges it, and why does that matter for building derived data?

options.text: It is deleted, so the consumer cannot be rerun later to get the same result
It is kept forever, so any new consumer can replay every past message
It is moved to an archive that new consumers read before live messages
It is kept until every possible future consumer has also acknowledged it

questions.explanation: In AMQP/JMS-style messaging, receiving a message is destructive: the acknowledgment causes it to be deleted from the broker. Unlike a batch job over read-only input, you cannot rerun the same consumer and expect the same result, and a newly added consumer only sees messages sent after it registered, because earlier ones are gone. Databases and files keep data until explicitly deleted, so a new client can read data written arbitrarily far in the past. This gap is what log-based brokers fill.

questions.question: What idea motivates log-based message brokers?

options.text: Pairing database-style durable storage with low-latency messaging notification
Removing the broker entirely so that producers send directly to consumers over UDP
Making every send synchronous so that producers wait for consumers to finish
Storing messages in a relational table that consumers poll periodically for changes

questions.explanation: Traditional brokers deliver promptly but delete messages after delivery; databases and files keep data durably but notify readers poorly. Log-based brokers combine the two: messages are durably appended to a log, so any consumer can reread history, and consumers are notified as soon as new messages are appended. Direct UDP messaging gives up durability, synchronous sends give up the decoupling of asynchronous delivery, and a polled table brings back the overhead of polling.

questions.question: In the sense used by log-based message brokers, what is a log?

options.text: An append-only sequence of records on disk
A searchable index that producers insert into and consumers query
A mutable file whose head producers overwrite in place
An in-memory buffer that is cleared once consumers read it

questions.explanation: A log is simply an append-only sequence of records on disk, the same structure used by log-structured storage engines, write-ahead logs, and replication. As a broker, a producer sends a message by appending it to the end of the log, and a consumer reads the log sequentially; at the end it waits to be notified of new messages, much like the Unix tool tail -f. Reading does not remove records, which is what lets several consumers read independently and replay.

questions.question: In a partitioned log-based broker such as Kafka, what does the broker assign to each message, and what ordering results?

options.text: A per-partition increasing offset, so order holds only within each partition
A global sequence number, so there is total order across the whole topic
An event timestamp, so messages are ordered by event time across the topic
A hash of the message key, so no ordering holds anywhere in the topic

questions.explanation: To scale beyond one disk, a topic is split into partitions, each a separate log on possibly different machines. Within each partition the broker assigns a monotonically increasing sequence number, the offset, to every message. Because a partition is append-only, its messages are totally ordered, but there is no ordering guarantee across partitions. Kafka, Amazon Kinesis Streams, and Twitter's DistributedLog work this way; partitioning lets them reach millions of messages per second, and replication gives fault tolerance.

questions.question: How does a log-based broker support both fan-out and load balancing across consumers?

options.text: Consumers read independently for fan-out; partitions go to group members for load balancing
Messages are deleted after delivery for fan-out; single messages are assigned for load balancing
The log is copied once per consumer for fan-out; single messages are assigned for load balancing
Fan-out is impossible with a log; whole partitions are assigned for load balancing

questions.explanation: Fan-out is trivial with a log because reading a message does not delete it, so several consumers can each read the whole log independently. For load balancing, instead of assigning individual messages, the broker assigns whole partitions to the nodes of a consumer group, and each node reads its partitions sequentially. The downsides of this coarse-grained scheme are that a topic can be shared by at most as many consumers as it has partitions, and one slow message holds up the rest of its partition (head-of-line blocking).

questions.question: When is a JMS/AMQP-style broker preferable to a log-based broker, and vice versa?

options.text: JMS/AMQP for expensive messages needing per-message parallelism; logs for fast, ordered, high-throughput ones
Logs for expensive messages needing per-message parallelism; JMS/AMQP for fast, ordered, high-throughput ones
Either style suits every workload equally; the choice is only a matter of vendor
JMS/AMQP when ordering matters most; logs when message ordering is irrelevant

questions.explanation: A JMS/AMQP broker assigns individual messages, so slow, expensive messages can be spread across many consumers one at a time; this suits workloads where ordering does not matter much. A log broker assigns whole partitions, each read sequentially by one consumer, so it preserves per-partition order and avoids per-message bookkeeping, which suits high throughput with fast-to-process messages where ordering matters. The cost is head-of-line blocking: one slow message delays the rest of its partition, and parallelism is capped by the number of partitions.

questions.question: Why does a log-based broker not need to track an acknowledgment for every single message?

options.text: Each partition is read sequentially, so one recorded offset shows what was processed
Messages are never lost once written, so the broker needs no record of consumer progress
Consumers acknowledge in fixed batches of exactly 1,000 messages
The broker deletes each message as soon as a consumer reads it

questions.explanation: Because a consumer reads a partition sequentially, every message below its current offset has been processed and every message above it has not. The broker only needs to record each consumer's offset periodically, which reduces bookkeeping and allows batching and pipelining, raising throughput. The offset works like the log sequence number in single-leader replication: the broker acts like a leader and the consumer like a follower that can reconnect and resume without skipping messages.

questions.question: In a log-based broker, a consumer node in a consumer group fails. What happens to the partitions it was reading?

options.text: Another node takes over its partitions from its last offset
The partition is left unassigned until the failed node returns
The messages in that partition are lost, since the failed node had already read them
The whole consumer group restarts from offset zero

questions.explanation: Another node in the group is assigned the failed node's partitions and starts reading at the last recorded offset. Messages are not lost, because reading never deleted them, and the group does not restart from offset zero. If the failed consumer had processed messages beyond its last recorded offset, those messages are processed a second time. Avoiding visible duplicates therefore needs atomic commit of output and offset, or idempotent processing.

questions.question: How does a log-based broker keep its append-only log from eventually filling the disk?

options.text: Old log segments are periodically deleted or moved to archive storage
Each message is deleted once every consumer acknowledges it, as in a JMS broker
Messages are compressed again and again, so the log never needs to delete anything
The broker refuses new writes once the disk is full

questions.explanation: The log is divided into segments, and from time to time old segments are deleted or moved to archive storage. The log therefore acts as a bounded, disk-based circular (ring) buffer: messages are kept regardless of whether they were consumed and discarded only when they age out. A consumer that falls so far behind that its offset points into a deleted segment misses messages. Because the buffer is on disk, it can be very large.

questions.question: Around 2017, a typical large hard drive held 6 TB with 150 MB/s of sequential write throughput. If a log-based broker writes messages to it at that full rate, roughly how long does it take to fill the drive?

options.text: About 11 hours
About 11 minutes
About 11 days
About 1 hour

questions.explanation: 6 TB is 6,000,000 MB; 6,000,000 MB divided by 150 MB/s is 40,000 seconds, about 11.1 hours (using decimal units). So even at the maximum write rate, one disk buffers about 11 hours of messages before old ones must be overwritten. The ratio stays the same with more disks and machines, since capacity and write bandwidth grow together. In practice deployments rarely use the full write bandwidth, so a log typically retains several days or even weeks of messages.

questions.question: When producers outpace consumers, a messaging system can drop messages, buffer them, or apply backpressure. Where does a log-based broker fit?

options.text: It buffers, using a large but fixed-size buffer limited by disk space
It applies backpressure, blocking producers once the disk is full
It drops each new incoming message once the disk is full
It fits none of the three options, being a different mechanism

questions.explanation: A log-based broker is a form of buffering with a large but fixed-size buffer, limited by available disk space. Producers are never blocked; instead, when old segments are deleted, a consumer that has fallen too far behind loses access to the oldest messages it still needed. So it buffers first and effectively drops the oldest data only when the buffer wraps around, not the newest arrivals. You can monitor consumer lag and alert before that happens.

questions.question: In a log-based broker that retains a large on-disk buffer, which operational advantages follow? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Consumer lag can be monitored, with time for an operator to fix a slow consumer
A consumer that falls too far behind affects only itself, not other consumers
A production log can be consumed experimentally for testing or debugging
A shut-down consumer holds a lock on its partition until it returns

questions.explanation: Because the log is large and reading is non-destructive, you can alert on how far a consumer is behind the head of the log and still have time to fix it, a lagging consumer harms only itself, and you can safely read a production log for development or debugging. When a consumer shuts down or crashes it stops using resources; only its offset remains. Traditional brokers differ: their queues for dead consumers keep accumulating messages and taking memory from active consumers unless someone deletes them.

optionExplanations.a: Lag is the distance between a consumer's offset and the head of the log. Long retention gives operators time to repair a slow consumer before the records it needs are deleted.
optionExplanations.b: Each consumer moves its own offset, so one lagging or failed consumer does not slow or block others. If it falls off the end of the buffer, only it misses messages.
optionExplanations.c: An experimental consumer reads production events with its own offset and removes nothing, so testing or debugging against real data has little risk to production.
optionExplanations.d: A stopped consumer leaves behind only its offset, not a lock. Holding a lock would block reassigning its partitions and waste resources, which is what the log design avoids.

questions.question: What properties of a log-based broker let consumers replay old messages?

options.text: Reading does not delete messages, and each consumer controls its own offset
The producer resends every message whenever a consumer requests a replay
Messages are deleted on read, but a backup copy is kept per consumer
The broker records each consumer's output so it can be returned again

questions.explanation: In a log-based broker, consuming is read-only: it does not change the log. The only side effect apart from the consumer's own output is that its offset advances, and the offset is under the consumer's control. You can, for example, start a copy of a consumer with yesterday's offsets, write output to a different location, and reprocess a day of messages, as often as you like with different code. This makes log-based messaging like batch processing, with derived data cleanly separated from input, and makes recovery from bugs easier.

questions.question: What observation shows that the connection between databases and streams is fundamental?

options.text: A replication log is a stream of write events
A database can serve as a broker by polling a table
A stream can be stored inside a relational table
Both logs and databases happen to be stored on disk

questions.explanation: A write to a database is itself an event that can be captured, stored, and processed. A leader's replication log is exactly such a stream of write events; followers apply it and end up with an accurate copy. State machine replication says the same: if every replica processes the same deterministic write events in the same order, all replicas end in the same state. Sharing disk storage or being able to put a stream in a table are superficial; the deep point is that database state is produced by a stream of changes.

questions.question: Why does a nontrivial application typically end up with several data systems, such as an OLTP database, a cache, a full-text index, and a data warehouse?

options.text: No single system meets every storage, query, and processing need
Databases are unreliable, so every record needs redundant copies elsewhere
Different teams prefer different products, regardless of requirements
Running a single system would always cost more than running several

questions.explanation: Each kind of system is optimized for different access patterns: an OLTP database for user requests, a cache for common reads, a full-text index for search, a warehouse for analytics. Each holds its own copy of the data in its own representation, so the copies must be kept in sync when data changes. Traditionally warehouses are synced by ETL batch jobs that dump, transform, and bulk-load the database; the streaming alternative is to propagate each change as it happens. Redundancy for reliability is handled by replication, not by using different kinds of systems.

questions.question: When keeping a database, a search index, and a cache in sync, what are 'dual writes'?

options.text: The application code itself writes each change to every system
The database writes each change twice to its own log for safety
The database replicates each change to two followers before it acks
A batch job copies a full database dump into each other system

questions.explanation: With dual writes, application code explicitly writes each change to every system, for example first to the database, then to the search index, then invalidating cache entries, or all concurrently. It is an alternative to slow periodic full dumps, but it has serious problems: concurrent clients' writes can reach the systems in different orders, leaving them permanently inconsistent, and one write can succeed while another fails. A full dump copied by a batch job is the ETL approach that dual writes try to replace.

questions.question: Besides the race in which concurrent writes reach the database and the search index in different orders, what other problem do dual writes have?

options.text: One write may succeed while the other fails, leaving the systems inconsistent
Every write is slowed by network latency that no design can avoid
The two systems store different encodings, so values cannot be compared
Clock skew between the two systems corrupts the stored timestamps

questions.explanation: This is a fault-tolerance problem rather than a concurrency problem: a crash or error can let the database write commit while the index write is lost, or vice versa. Ensuring both succeed or both fail is the atomic commit problem, which is expensive to solve (for example with two-phase commit). The better structure is a single leader whose ordered change log the other systems follow, as change data capture provides.

questions.question: Why was it historically hard to make a search index follow a database's changes via its replication log?

options.text: The replication log was an internal detail, not a documented public API
Search indexes cannot apply writes in the order a database made them
Database licences contractually forbid reading the replication log
Replication logs are encrypted so that only followers can read them

questions.explanation: For decades, replication logs were considered an internal implementation detail; clients were supposed to use the data model and query language, and many databases offered no documented way to get the log of changes. That made it hard to replicate changes to another technology such as a search index, cache, or warehouse. Change data capture (CDC) addresses this by observing all writes and extracting them in a form other systems can consume, ideally as a stream.

questions.question: What does change data capture (CDC) do to the relationship between a source database and derived systems, and why is a log-based broker a good transport?

options.text: The source is the leader, the rest followers; a log broker keeps changes in order
All systems become equal peers; a JMS broker is best because it redelivers messages
The search index becomes the leader; any broker works because order is irrelevant
Leaders disappear entirely; no broker is needed because systems write to each other

questions.explanation: CDC makes the database the changes are captured from the leader (the system of record) and turns derived systems such as search indexes and warehouses into followers that apply the same changes in the same order. If the order is preserved, the derived data matches the source. A log-based broker suits this because it keeps messages in order within a partition, whereas load balancing with redelivery in a JMS/AMQP broker can reorder them. CDC is usually asynchronous, so followers may lag.

questions.question: How can database triggers implement change data capture, and how does that compare with parsing the replication log?

options.text: Triggers fill a changelog table but are fragile and slow; log parsing is more robust
Triggers are robust and cheap, whereas parsing the replication log is fragile and slow
The two methods are equally robust and have identical performance overheads
Only triggers can work, because a replication log cannot be parsed externally

questions.explanation: With triggers, you register triggers that observe all changes to data tables and add matching entries to a changelog table. They tend to be fragile and add significant performance overhead to every write. Parsing the replication log can be more robust, though it has its own challenges, such as handling schema changes. Many production CDC tools read the log: PostgreSQL's write-ahead log, MySQL's binlog, or MongoDB's oplog.

questions.question: What do CDC tools such as Bottled Water (PostgreSQL), Maxwell and Debezium (MySQL), and Mongoriver (MongoDB) have in common, as described around 2017?

options.text: They read the database's own write-ahead log, binlog, or oplog
They install triggers that copy each change into a changelog table
They poll every table periodically and diff successive snapshots
They require applications to dual-write every change to Kafka

questions.explanation: These tools capture changes from the database's internal log: Bottled Water decodes PostgreSQL's write-ahead log through its decoding API, Maxwell and Debezium parse the MySQL binlog, and Mongoriver reads the MongoDB oplog; GoldenGate offers similar facilities for Oracle. Reading the log gives changes in the exact order they were committed without trigger overhead and without changing the application. Polling and diffing snapshots is slow and misses intermediate states, and dual writes are what CDC is meant to replace.

questions.question: Why does a new CDC consumer, such as a new full-text index, usually start from a consistent snapshot rather than by replaying the whole change log?

options.text: Keeping all changes needs too much disk and replay is slow, so the log is truncated
The change log is encrypted, and only the database's own followers hold the key to read it
Replaying the changes would modify them, so the source data would be altered
The change log carries no ordering, so replaying it gives an undefined result

questions.explanation: With the complete history of changes, you could rebuild the database by replay, but keeping every change forever usually takes too much disk and replay would take too long, so the log is truncated. Applying only recent changes would miss items not recently updated, so the new consumer needs a consistent snapshot of the whole database. The snapshot must correspond to a known offset in the change log, so you know where to start applying changes afterwards. Log compaction offers an alternative that avoids taking a fresh snapshot.

questions.question: In a log-structured storage engine or a log-based broker, what does log compaction keep, and how is a deleted key represented?

options.text: The latest value per key; a deletion is a tombstone (null) that removes the key
The oldest records regardless of key; a tombstone marks a record to keep
The sum of all values per key; a tombstone is a checksum of the merged value
The first value written per key; a tombstone marks the key's first insert

questions.explanation: Compaction periodically finds log records with the same key, throws away older duplicates, and keeps only the most recent update for each key, running in the background. A delete is written as an update with a special null value, a tombstone, which causes the key to be removed during compaction. As a result, the space a compacted log needs depends on the current contents of the database, not on how many writes ever happened. Kafka supports this for topics.

questions.question: What property of CDC events lets a log-compacted topic be used to rebuild a full copy of the database?

options.text: Each change carries a primary key and the full new value, replacing the old one
Each change carries only the difference from the previous value for that key
Each change is delivered at most once, so the topic never holds duplicates to compact away
Each change carries a monotonically increasing wall-clock timestamp

questions.explanation: If every change has a primary key and every update for a key replaces the previous value, only the latest write per key matters, and compaction can safely discard the rest. The compacted log is then guaranteed to contain the latest value of every key, so a new derived system such as a search index can start a consumer at offset 0, scan the whole topic, and get a full copy of the database without taking another snapshot of the source. Deltas would need all earlier events, so they cannot be compacted this way.

questions.question: Which of these were examples (around 2017) of databases offering change streams as a first-class interface rather than retrofitted CDC?

options.text: RethinkDB query-change subscriptions, and Firebase and CouchDB change feeds
Read repair in Cassandra and Riak, which pushes each change to clients
Trigger-based changelog tables, offered as a supported public API
MySQL binlog parsing by Maxwell and Debezium, feeding changes into Kafka

questions.explanation: Databases increasingly support change streams directly: RethinkDB lets queries subscribe to notifications when their results change, Firebase and CouchDB synchronize data through a change feed that applications can use, Meteor uses the MongoDB oplog to update user interfaces, and VoltDB lets transactions export data as a stream. Read repair is a replica-consistency technique that fixes stale replicas during reads; it is not a change feed. Trigger-based changelog tables and binlog parsing by tools such as Maxwell and Debezium are retrofitted CDC: they extract changes from mechanisms the database did not design as a public change interface.

questions.question: What is Kafka Connect, in the context of change data capture?

options.text: A connector framework that brings database changes into Kafka and exports Kafka data
The wire protocol that Kafka clients use to open their connections to brokers
A SQL query language for running ad hoc analytical queries over Kafka topics
A partitioning scheme that decides which partition each new message is written to

questions.explanation: Kafka Connect is an effort to integrate CDC tools for many database systems with Kafka. Source connectors bring change events into Kafka; sink connectors export Kafka data to other databases and indexes. Once changes are in Kafka they can update derived systems such as search indexes and feed stream processors, replacing custom dual-write code with reusable connectors over an ordered, durable log.

questions.question: In which community was event sourcing developed?

options.text: The domain-driven design (DDD) community
The stream processing community around Kafka
The relational database research community
The functional programming community

questions.explanation: Event sourcing was developed in the domain-driven design community. Like CDC, it stores all changes to application state as a log of change events, but at the application level: the application is built on immutable events describing what happened in the domain, and current state is derived from them. It is independent of any tool; it can be built on a dedicated event store, a conventional database, or a log-based broker such as Kafka.

questions.question: What is the biggest difference between change data capture and event sourcing?

options.text: CDC extracts low-level changes from a mutable database; event sourcing builds on immutable app-level events
CDC records app-level events in an event store; event sourcing extracts low-level changes from a database
They are the same technique described under two different names
CDC needs an append-only store, while event sourcing lets events be updated freely

questions.explanation: Both store changes as a log of events, but at different levels of abstraction. In CDC the application uses the database mutably, updating and deleting at will, and the change log is extracted at a low level (e.g. from the replication log) without the application knowing. In event sourcing, application logic is explicitly built on immutable events written to an append-only event store, where updates and deletes are discouraged or prohibited; events describe things that happened at the application level, such as 'student cancelled their course enrollment', rather than low-level row changes.

questions.question: What does event sourcing offer as a data-modeling technique? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Recording user actions as immutable events, which is more meaningful than recording their effects
Making it easier to evolve the application over time
Helping debugging by showing after the fact why something happened
Guarding against hardware faults by replicating each event to several machines

questions.explanation: Recording 'student cancelled their course enrollment' expresses the intent of one action neutrally, whereas the side effects (a row deleted from enrollments, a reason added to a feedback table) embed assumptions about how the data will be used. A new feature, such as offering the freed place to the next person on the waiting list, can be chained off the existing event. Event sourcing also aids debugging and guards against application bugs, because the events can be reprocessed. It does not by itself provide replication against hardware faults.

optionExplanations.a: An immutable event records intent, such as cancelling an enrollment, rather than only table changes. Later code can derive different effects from the same meaningful fact.
optionExplanations.b: New features can replay old events into a new view without rewriting the authoritative history, so future read models are not tied to past storage decisions.
optionExplanations.c: The event sequence explains how the current state arose, so unexpected outcomes can be traced back to the user actions that caused them. A mutable snapshot loses that history.
optionExplanations.d: Replicating data protects against hardware loss, but choosing event sourcing does not provide it. Durability and replica count remain separate infrastructure decisions.

questions.question: Which existing data-modeling ideas does an event-sourcing event log resemble?

options.text: The chronicle data model, and the fact table of a star schema
The normalized current-state tables of the relational model
The vertices and edges of a property graph model
A key-value store whose values are overwritten in place

questions.explanation: An event log is an append-only record of immutable facts over time, like the chronicle data model and like the fact table in a data-warehouse star schema, where each row records an event such as a sale. Normalized current-state tables and in-place key-value overwrites describe the latest state rather than history, and a graph model describes relationships between entities. Dedicated databases such as Event Store support event sourcing, but a conventional database or a log-based broker can also be used.

questions.question: On an event-sourced shopping website, why can't the application simply show users the raw event log?

options.text: Users expect current state, such as their cart's contents, not the change history
Event logs are too large, so any transformation of them must lose information
Event logs are encrypted, so they must be decrypted before they are displayed
Events are mutable, so the log may change while the user is reading it

questions.explanation: Users want to see the current contents of their cart, not an append-only list of every change they made to it. An event-sourced application therefore transforms the event log (how data is written) into application state suited to display (how data is read). The transformation may use arbitrary logic but should be deterministic, so it can be rerun to derive the same state from the log, for example after a code change.

questions.question: Log compaction keeps only the latest event for each key. Why does that work for CDC but not in the same way for event sourcing?

options.text: CDC events hold the full new record; event-sourcing events record intent, not state
CDC events are smaller than event-sourcing events, so they compress far better on disk
Event-sourcing events never carry keys, so a compactor has no way to group them together
CDC logs are never replayed by any consumer, so losing their old events does not matter

questions.explanation: A CDC update usually carries the entire new version of the record, so the latest event for a primary key fully determines its value and older ones can be discarded. Event-sourcing events record user intent, such as 'item added to cart', not the resulting state, so later events do not override earlier ones and the full history is needed to rebuild state. Event-sourced systems often store snapshots of derived state to speed up reads and crash recovery, but only as an optimization; the intention is to keep all raw events and be able to reprocess them.

questions.question: In event sourcing, what is a user request called when it first arrives and may still fail validation, and what does it become once accepted?

options.text: A command; once validated and accepted it becomes an immutable event
An event; once validated it becomes a mutable command
A tentative event; it becomes a command after consumers approve it
A command; it stays a command forever, since events are only views

questions.explanation: A request initially is a command: it may still fail, for example because the username is taken or the seat already reserved. The application validates it; if the command is accepted, it becomes an event, which is durable and immutable, a fact. If the customer later changes or cancels a reservation, the fact that they held it remains true, and the cancellation is a separate event added later.

questions.question: In event sourcing, why must a command usually be validated synchronously, before it becomes an event?

options.text: A consumer cannot reject an event: it is already in the log and others may have read it
Consumers are free to reject events later, so validation could safely happen afterwards
The log validates every event itself at append time, so the application need not
Validation is unnecessary in event sourcing, because every event is a fact

questions.explanation: By the time a consumer sees an event it is an immutable part of the log and may already have been read by other consumers, so it cannot be rejected. Validation must therefore happen before the event exists, for example in a serializable transaction that atomically validates the command and publishes the event. Alternatively, the request can be split into a tentative-reservation event and a later confirmation event, which lets validation run asynchronously.

questions.question: How can mutable database state be reconciled with an append-only log of immutable events?

options.text: State is the result of the events that changed it, so they are two sides of one coin
Mutable state is abandoned entirely, and every query scans the raw event log
The log is discarded once state is updated, because the two conflict
They cannot be reconciled, so a system must commit to one of the two models

questions.explanation: Whenever state changes, it is the result of the events that changed it: available seats result from processed reservations, an account balance from credits and debits, a response-time graph from individual requests. Even as things are done and undone, the events still occurred. Mutable state and an immutable changelog are thus two sides of the same coin: the log records how state evolved, and the state is a convenient, read-optimized digest of the log. Neither needs to be abandoned.

questions.question: What is the calculus analogy for the relationship between application state and an event stream?

options.text: State integrates the event stream over time; the stream is state's derivative
State is the derivative of the event stream; the stream is the integral of state
Each is the derivative of the other, so the relationship is fully symmetric
The analogy is exact, so even the second derivative of state is meaningful

questions.explanation: Integrating an event stream over time accumulates the changes into the current state; differentiating state with respect to time yields the stream of changes. The analogy has limits, for example the second derivative of state does not seem meaningful, but it is a useful way to think about state and changelogs. It also explains joins: the change stream of a materialized join follows the product rule, so a change on either input joins with the current state of the other.

questions.question: In an event-sourced design, what is the durable source of truth and what is the database?

options.text: The event log is the source of truth; the database is a derived cache
The database is the truth and the log is merely a cache of it
The two are equally authoritative, so either may be trusted
The application code is the authority, rather than either the log or the database

questions.explanation: If you treat the log of events as the system of record, all mutable state is derived from it, which makes data flow easier to reason about. In Pat Helland's phrasing, the truth is the log, and the database is a cache of a subset of it: the latest value of each record and index. Storing the changelog durably makes state reproducible. Log compaction bridges the two views by keeping only the latest version of each record.

questions.question: How does financial bookkeeping illustrate the value of immutability?

options.text: Entries are appended to a ledger; a mistake is fixed by a compensating entry
Accountants erase the incorrect entry and write the corrected one in its place
Accountants delete the affected period's entries and recompute them from scratch
Accountants keep only current balances, overwriting them as transactions occur

questions.explanation: Accountants have used immutability for centuries: each transaction is recorded in an append-only ledger, and accounts such as profit and loss are derived by adding up the ledger. A mistake is not erased; a compensating transaction, such as a refund, is added, and the incorrect entry remains for auditing. The same reasoning applies to software: if buggy code writes bad data, recovery is much easier with an append-only log of immutable events than when the code destructively overwrote data.

questions.question: On a shopping site a customer adds an item to their cart and then removes it. Why is an append-only event log more useful here than a database that deletes the cart row?

options.text: Fulfillment sees the events cancel out; analytics sees the item was considered
The events cancel out completely, so nothing of value is lost by deleting the row
The log lets fulfillment ship the item, because the add event remains recorded
The log matters only for auditing, and analytics gains nothing from the pair

questions.explanation: Immutable events capture more than current state. For order fulfillment the removal cancels the addition, but for analytics it is useful that the customer considered the item and decided against it; perhaps they will buy it later or found a substitute. A database that deletes the item on removal loses that information. Fulfillment derives the cart's current state from both events, so it does not ship the removed item.

questions.question: What is the main benefit of deriving several read-oriented views from the same immutable event log?

options.text: A new feature can build its own read view from the log beside existing ones
Every view reflects each event synchronously, so no derived view is ever stale
Only one schema is needed, because every view must share the log's write format
Every new feature requires a coordinated schema migration of all existing views

questions.explanation: Separating mutable state from the immutable log works like having several consumers of one stream: Druid ingests directly from Kafka, Pistachio uses Kafka as a commit log, and Kafka Connect sinks export to various databases and indexes. To present existing data in a new way, you build a separate read-optimized view from the log and run it alongside the existing systems without modifying them, which is often easier than a complex schema migration; the old view can later be shut down. The views are usually updated asynchronously, so they can lag, and each can have its own schema.

questions.question: What is the name of the idea of separating the form in which data is written from the one or more forms in which it is read?

options.text: Command query responsibility segregation (CQRS)
Change data capture (CDC) from the replication log
Two-phase commit (2PC) across the write and read stores
Log compaction of superseded values for each key

questions.explanation: Command query responsibility segregation (CQRS) separates the write model from one or more read models. Much of the complexity of schema design and indexing comes from supporting particular query patterns, so writing data in one form (such as an event log) and deriving read-optimized views gives flexibility. It also makes the normalization-versus-denormalization debate largely irrelevant: denormalizing a read view is fine because the translation from the log keeps it consistent. CDC is a way to extract changes, 2PC is an atomic commit protocol, and log compaction discards superseded values.

questions.question: What is the biggest downside of event sourcing and change data capture?

options.text: That consumers are asynchronous, so a reader may not see their own write
That the log grows without bound, and the only remedy is deleting old events
That events are mutable, and the solution is adding checksums
That events arrive unordered even within a partition, and the solution is timestamps

questions.explanation: Consumers of the event log are usually asynchronous, so a user may append a write and then read from a derived view that does not reflect it yet (a read-your-writes problem). One fix is to update the read view synchronously with the log append, which needs a transaction: either keep the log and the view in one storage system, or use a distributed transaction. Another is to build linearizable storage on total order broadcast. The log need not grow without bound (compaction and retention exist), events are immutable by design, and ordering within a partition is preserved.

questions.question: With event sourcing, how can a user action that would otherwise change data in several places be made atomic?

options.text: Design the event to describe the whole action, so a single log append suffices
Take two-phase locks on every affected object before appending the event
Write each affected object separately and reconcile any differences later
Use more multi-object transactions, since derived views multiply the writes

questions.explanation: Much of the need for multi-object transactions comes from one user action changing data in several places. In event sourcing you can design an event as a self-contained description of the action, so the action needs only one write, appending the event to the log, which is easy to make atomic. If the log and the application state are partitioned the same way, a single-threaded consumer per partition needs no concurrency control for writes, because the log defines a serial order of events. Events touching several partitions need more work.

questions.question: What mainly determines whether it is feasible to keep an immutable history of all changes forever?

options.text: Churn: many updates and deletes on a small dataset bloat history
The size of the current dataset alone, regardless of how often it changes
Whether the data is stored on solid-state drives or on spinning disks
Whether the database uses a relational or a document data model

questions.explanation: It depends on how much the dataset churns. Workloads that mostly add data and rarely update or delete are easy to keep immutable. Workloads with a high rate of updates and deletes on a comparatively small dataset can make the immutable history prohibitively large, cause fragmentation, and make compaction and garbage-collection performance crucial for operational robustness. Storage media and data model do not change this basic ratio of history to current state.

questions.question: Despite immutability, when might you need to truly delete data from an event history, rather than append an event marking it deleted?

options.text: When privacy law, data-protection rules, or a data leak require it
Whenever disk usage grows, because compaction alone can never reclaim space
Whenever an auditor asks for a record of who changed which data
Never, because appending a deletion event satisfies every requirement

questions.explanation: Administrative reasons can require real deletion: privacy regulations may require deleting a user's personal data after they close their account, data-protection law may require removing erroneous information, or a leak of sensitive data may need containing. Appending a 'deleted' event leaves the original in history, so you need to rewrite history as if the data were never written; Datomic calls this excision and Fossil calls it shunning. True deletion is hard because copies live in storage engines, filesystems, SSDs, and backups; it mostly makes data harder to retrieve rather than impossible. Auditing is a reason to keep history, not delete it.

questions.question: Once you have a stream of events, which of these are broad options for what to do with it? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Write events into a database, cache, search index, or other derived store
Push alerts, notifications, or dashboard updates to people
Transform input streams into new output streams
Wait for the unbounded stream to finish before doing anything with it

questions.explanation: There are three broad options: write the events into a database, cache, search index, or other store that other clients query; push them to people as email alerts, push notifications, or a real-time dashboard; or process input streams into new output streams, possibly through a pipeline of several stages. A stream processor reads its input read-only and writes output elsewhere append-only. Waiting for the stream to end is not an option, because an unbounded stream never ends.

optionExplanations.a: A stream processor can maintain a derived database, cache, or index by applying each event as an incremental state change. The store serves the resulting current view.
optionExplanations.b: Events can trigger human-facing effects such as alerts or dashboard updates when a monitored condition changes. This is a terminal consumer rather than another data stream.
optionExplanations.c: Operators may filter, join, or aggregate events and append the results to downstream streams. Chained streams form a reusable processing pipeline.
optionExplanations.d: Waiting for an unbounded stream to finish means processing never begins because no final record exists. Streaming systems must act incrementally rather than await completion.

questions.question: Which aspects of batch processing carry over to stream processing essentially unchanged?

options.text: Partitioning and parallelization patterns, and simple transforming and filtering
Sorting the whole input by key and running sort-merge joins over the sorted result
Restarting a failed job from the very beginning of its input after any crash
Keeping all of a job's output hidden until the job has completely finished

questions.explanation: Stream processors partition and parallelize work much like MapReduce and dataflow engines, and basic mapping operations such as transforming and filtering records work the same. The crucial difference is that a stream never ends. Sorting makes no sense on an unbounded dataset, so sort-merge joins cannot be used. Fault tolerance must change too: restarting from the beginning is fine for a job that has run a few minutes, but not for a stream job that has run for years, and output cannot be hidden until a job finishes that never finishes.

questions.question: Stream processing has long been used for monitoring, where an organization wants an alert when certain things happen. Which of these are monitoring applications in that sense? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Fraud detection that blocks a credit card when its usage pattern suddenly changes
Trading systems that execute trades by rules as market prices change
Manufacturing systems that quickly identify a malfunctioning factory machine
Weather systems that publish one forecast a day from accumulated readings

questions.explanation: Monitoring applications watch events continuously and react when a condition occurs: fraud detection, rule-based trading, factory machine monitoring, and military or intelligence systems watching for signs of attack. They need sophisticated pattern matching and correlation. A forecast produced once a day from accumulated data is periodic batch analysis, even when its inputs are sensor readings.

optionExplanations.a: Fraud detection continuously compares new transactions with expected behavior and may block a card at once. A delayed batch report would arrive after the harm was done.
optionExplanations.b: Trading systems watch market price events and act on them under timing-sensitive rules. Reacting promptly to a changing condition is the monitoring pattern.
optionExplanations.c: Factory telemetry must reveal an abnormal machine state quickly enough to intervene. Continuous evaluation of events distinguishes it from retrospective reporting.
optionExplanations.d: A forecast published on a fixed daily schedule is periodic batch analysis, not continuous monitoring, even though its inputs come from sensors.

questions.question: What is complex event processing (CEP), and roughly when did it emerge?

options.text: A 1990s approach that searches streams for event patterns, like a regex over events
A 2010s approach that computes rolling averages, like SQL GROUP BY over windows
A 1970s approach that sorts event logs in batch, much like an external merge sort
A 2000s approach that replicates events between databases, like log shipping

questions.explanation: CEP was developed in the 1990s for applications that search event streams for particular patterns. Just as a regular expression finds patterns of characters in a string, CEP rules find patterns of events in a stream. Patterns are usually described in a declarative language like SQL or through a graphical interface; the engine keeps a state machine that does the matching and emits a 'complex event' describing each detected pattern. Rolling averages and other aggregates are the focus of stream analytics instead.

questions.question: How does complex event processing (CEP) reverse the usual relationship between queries and data?

options.text: Queries are stored long-term and the event data flows past them
Data is stored long-term and queries are transient, as in a database
Neither queries nor data are kept; each event is matched and forgotten
Both queries and data are stored permanently, so either can be replayed

questions.explanation: A normal database stores data persistently and treats queries as transient: a query arrives, the database finds matching data, and forgets the query. CEP engines reverse these roles: queries are stored long-term, and events from the input streams continuously flow past them in search of a query whose pattern they match. Implementations include Esper, IBM InfoSphere Streams, Apama, TIBCO StreamBase, and SQLstream. The same inversion appears in search on streams.

questions.question: Where does the boundary between complex event processing and stream analytics fall?

options.text: Analytics cares about aggregates rather than specific event sequences
The boundary is sharp: CEP is declarative and analytics is imperative
Analytics finds event sequences while CEP computes the aggregates
The two are indistinguishable, being one and the same technique

questions.explanation: The boundary is blurry, but as a rule CEP looks for specific sequences of events, while analytics focuses on aggregations and statistical metrics over many events: event rates per time interval, rolling averages, and comparisons with earlier periods to spot trends. For example, you might compute the average queries per second over the last 5 minutes and the 99th-percentile response time in that period. Averaging over a few minutes smooths out second-to-second noise while still showing changes promptly. The interval aggregated over is called a window.

questions.question: Stream analytics sometimes uses Bloom filters, HyperLogLog, and percentile estimators. What does this imply about stream processing?

options.text: They trade exactness for memory; stream processing is not inherently approximate
Stream processing is inherently lossy, so approximate algorithms are always mandatory
These algorithms give exact answers, merely using less memory than exact methods
Approximate algorithms are used only in batch jobs and never in stream processors

questions.explanation: Probabilistic algorithms, such as Bloom filters for set membership, HyperLogLog for cardinality, and percentile estimators, give approximate results but need far less memory in the stream processor than exact algorithms. Their use leads some people to think stream processing is always lossy and inexact, which is wrong: nothing about stream processing is inherently approximate, and probabilistic algorithms are merely an optimization.

questions.question: How does maintaining a materialized view from a stream (for example from CDC or an event-sourcing log) differ from typical stream analytics?

options.text: It may need all events since the beginning, not just a recent window
It needs only a shorter window than analytics, because views stay small
It needs no state at all, because each event is written straight through
It cannot be done with a stream processor, only with periodic batch jobs

questions.explanation: Keeping caches, search indexes, or event-sourced application state up to date are cases of maintaining a materialized view: a derived view of a dataset, updated whenever the data changes. Unlike analytics, considering only events in a recent time window is usually not enough; the view may need all events over an arbitrary period, apart from obsolete ones discarded by log compaction, in effect a window reaching back to the beginning of time. That runs counter to analytics frameworks designed for limited windows; Samza and Kafka Streams support it using Kafka's log compaction.

questions.question: How does search on streams (for example with Elasticsearch's percolator) differ from a conventional search engine?

options.text: Queries are stored in advance; each new document is run past them
Documents are indexed first, and queries are then run over that index
Each query runs once over the whole history and is then discarded
It looks for patterns spanning several events, not single documents

questions.explanation: A conventional search engine indexes documents first and then runs queries over the index. Searching a stream turns this around: queries are formulated in advance and stored, and each incoming document runs past them, as when media monitoring watches news feeds for mentions of companies, or a real estate site alerts users to new matching properties. To avoid testing every document against every query, the queries themselves can be indexed. Searching for patterns spanning several events is complex event processing; stream search matches individual events.

questions.question: Why don't we normally think of actor frameworks as stream processors? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Actors primarily organize concurrency; streams primarily manage data
Actor messages are often ephemeral and one-to-one; logs are durable and shared
Actor graphs may be cyclic; stream pipelines usually have defined acyclic derivations
Actors cannot process messages, unlike stream operators

questions.explanation: Actor frameworks and stream processors both use messages, but they differ in purpose and structure: actors mainly manage concurrency and distributed execution, while stream processing is a data management technique; actor communication is often ephemeral and one-to-one, while event logs are durable and multi-subscriber; and actors may communicate cyclically, while stream processors usually form acyclic pipelines. You can process streams with actors, but many actor frameworks do not guarantee delivery after crashes, so processing is not fault-tolerant without extra retry logic.

optionExplanations.a: Actor frameworks mainly structure concurrent components and distributed execution, whereas stream processors mainly describe how data is transformed and derived.
optionExplanations.b: Actor messages are often transient and addressed to a single actor, whereas a log stream is retained and can be read independently by many consumers, which changes recovery.
optionExplanations.c: Actors can exchange messages in arbitrary cyclic patterns, while stream jobs usually form acyclic pipelines where each stream is derived from well-defined inputs.
optionExplanations.d: Processing messages is the core purpose of an actor, so being unable to do so is not the difference. The differences are in purpose, durability, and topology.

questions.question: When a batch job breaks events down by time (for example, counts per hour), which timestamp should it use, and why?

options.text: The timestamp embedded in each event, so reruns are deterministic and reflect real time
The processing machine's system clock, so results reflect when the job actually ran
The broker's clock at ingestion, because the broker's clock is always synchronized
A logical Lamport counter, because wall-clock time has no meaning in batch jobs

questions.explanation: A batch job may process a year of historical events in a few minutes; the timeline of interest is the year, not the few minutes of processing.
