So it uses the timestamp embedded in each event; the system clock of the processing machine is unrelated to when the events occurred. Using event timestamps also makes processing deterministic: rerunning the job on the same input yields the same result.

questions.question: Many stream processing frameworks use which clock to assign events to windows, and when does that break down?

options.text: The processing machine's clock; it breaks down when processing lags far behind
The event's embedded timestamp; it breaks down whenever any device clock is slightly skewed
A logical clock; it breaks down once the cluster grows beyond a few nodes
The broker's ingestion time; it never breaks down under any conditions

questions.explanation: Many frameworks window by processing time, the local system clock of the machine doing the processing. It is simple and reasonable when the delay between creating and processing an event is negligible, but it breaks down when processing happens noticeably later than the event: through queueing, network faults, contention in the broker or processor, a consumer restart, or reprocessing past events after a fault or bug fix. Windowing by event time avoids those artifacts but raises its own problem of knowing when a window is complete.

questions.question: A user makes a web request handled by server A, then a second request handled by server B. Each server emits an event to a message broker, but B's event reaches the broker first. In what order do stream processors see the events?

options.text: B's event first, then A's, even though A's request happened first
A's event first, because the broker reorders events by occurrence time
Only B's event, because A's late-arriving event is discarded
Both at once, because the broker assigns identical timestamps to events of one user

questions.explanation: Message delays can reorder events: processors see events in the order they reached the broker, so B's event comes first even though A's request happened earlier. Brokers do not reorder by occurrence time, and a late event is not discarded automatically. Stream algorithms must be written explicitly to cope with such timing and ordering issues, for example by windowing on event timestamps.

questions.question: The Star Wars films were released as Episodes IV, V, VI, then I, II, III, then VII. How does this illustrate event time versus processing time?

options.text: The episode number is like event time; the date you watch a film is processing time
Release order is like a log's offset order, which always matches event-time order
The viewing date is like event time; the episode number is processing time
The episode number is like a window size; the release date is the window start

questions.explanation: If you watch the films in release order, the order in which you process them differs from the order of their story. The episode number is like the event timestamp (when things happened in the narrative), and the date you watched is like processing time. Humans cope with such discontinuities easily, but stream processing algorithms must be written explicitly to handle events that arrive out of event-time order.

questions.question: A stream processor measures requests per second using processing time. It is redeployed, is down for a minute, and then works through the backlog. The real request rate was steady. What does its rate graph show?

options.text: A spike as the backlog is processed, although the real rate was steady
A steady rate throughout, matching the real request rate exactly
A dip during the outage, then a steady rate, since the backlog is dropped on restart
A gap with no data, then an accurate steady rate afterwards

questions.explanation: Windowing by processing time counts each event when it is processed, not when it occurred. After the restart, a minute's backlog is processed quickly, so the processing-time windows suddenly contain many more requests, showing a spike that did not happen in reality. Confusing event time and processing time produces bad data like this; counting by event timestamps would show the steady rate.

questions.question: When windowing by event time, what correctness problem do late events create for a window whose result has already been emitted?

options.text: Late events can make the previously emitted result incomplete
The windows overlap, so some events are counted twice over
The window counter overflows before it can be reported
The late events are silently added to whichever window is open when they arrive

questions.explanation: With event-time windows you can never be sure you have received every event for a window: some may be buffered on another machine or delayed by a network interruption. Advancing processing time does not prove a window is complete. When a straggler for an already-emitted window arrives, the earlier result is incomplete, so you need a policy: ignore stragglers (tracking how many are dropped) or publish a corrected value. An event-time window assigns a late event by its own timestamp, not to whichever window happens to be open (that is processing-time behavior), and late events cause undercounting, not double-counting or overflow.

questions.question: What are the two broad options for handling straggler events that arrive after their event-time window was declared complete?

options.text: Ignore them while tracking how many were dropped, or publish a corrected result
Buffer them indefinitely, or crash the process so that it restarts cleanly
Re-sort the entire stream by timestamp, or discard the whole affected window
Extend every window forever, or shrink windows down to zero length

questions.explanation: You can ignore stragglers, since they are usually a small fraction of events, tracking the number dropped as a metric and alerting if it grows; or you can publish a correction, an updated value for the window including stragglers, possibly retracting the earlier output. Some systems also send a special message meaning 'no more events with timestamps earlier than t' to trigger windows, but with many producers each having its own threshold, consumers must track every producer individually.

questions.question: A mobile app records usage events while offline and uploads them hours later. Which timestamp best describes when each user interaction happened, and what is its weakness?

options.text: The device's clock at interaction time; meaningful, but it may be set wrong
The server's receive time; meaningful, and always accurate for the interaction itself
The broker's offset; it measures the elapsed time between events exactly
The processing time; it matches the interaction, since uploads are always fast

questions.explanation: Buffered events reach the server as extremely delayed stragglers. The timestamp that describes the user interaction is the time it occurred according to the device's clock, but a user-controlled device's clock often cannot be trusted, since it may be set wrong accidentally or on purpose. The server's receive time is more likely to be accurate because you control the server, but it describes when the upload arrived, possibly hours or days after the interaction. An offset is a position in the log, not a time.

questions.question: To correct for an untrustworthy device clock, which three timestamps should be logged for each event, and how is the clock offset estimated?

options.text: Device event time, device send time, server receive time; offset is receive minus send
Device event time, server receive time, processing time; offset is processing minus receive
Server receive time only; the device clock is ignored, so no offset is needed
Device event time and device send time; the offset is send time minus event time

questions.explanation: Log when the event occurred (device clock), when it was sent (device clock), and when it was received (server clock). Subtracting the send time from the receive time estimates the offset between device and server clocks, assuming network delay is negligible relative to the accuracy needed. Applying that offset to the event time estimates when the event truly occurred, assuming the device's offset did not change between the event and the send. Send minus event time measures only how long the event was buffered.

questions.question: What defines a tumbling window?

options.text: A fixed length, with every event in exactly one window
A fixed length, with windows that overlap their neighbours
Variable length; a window closes after a period of inactivity
All events within some interval of each other, with no fixed boundaries

questions.explanation: A tumbling window has a fixed length and non-overlapping boundaries, so every event belongs to exactly one window. With 1-minute tumbling windows, events stamped 10:03:00 to 10:03:59 form one window and 10:04:00 to 10:04:59 the next; you can assign an event by rounding its timestamp down to the minute. Overlapping fixed windows are hopping windows, inactivity-based ones are session windows, and windows relative to each event are sliding windows.

questions.question: What defines a hopping window?

options.text: A fixed length, but windows overlap in order to smooth results
Variable length; a window closes after a period of inactivity
A fixed length, with windows that never overlap their neighbours
All events within some interval of each other, with no fixed boundaries

questions.explanation: A hopping window has a fixed length but starts more often than its length, so windows overlap and results are smoothed. A 5-minute window with a 1-minute hop covers 10:03:00 to 10:07:59, then 10:04:00 to 10:08:59, and so on. You can implement it by computing 1-minute tumbling windows and aggregating several adjacent ones. Hopping windows still have fixed boundaries, unlike sliding windows.

questions.question: In stream processing, what defines a sliding window?

options.text: All events that occur within some interval of each other, with no fixed boundaries
Fixed, non-overlapping boundaries, assigned by rounding timestamps down
Variable length; the window ends when the user has been inactive for a while
A fixed length, with new windows starting at fixed hop intervals

questions.explanation: A sliding window contains all events that occur within some interval of each other. A 5-minute sliding window would group events at 10:03:39 and 10:08:12, because they are less than 5 minutes apart, whereas 5-minute tumbling or hopping windows would not, because their boundaries are fixed. It can be implemented by keeping a buffer of events sorted by time and removing events as they expire from the window. Hopping windows are the common confusion: they overlap but still have fixed boundaries.

questions.question: What defines a session window, making it unlike tumbling, hopping, and sliding windows?

options.text: No fixed duration — it groups one user's events by inactivity gap
It has a fixed duration but is allowed to overlap with itself
It groups all users together rather than one window per user
It covers all events within a fixed interval of each other, like a sliding window

questions.explanation: A session window has no fixed duration. It groups together all events for the same user that occur close together in time, and it ends when the user has been inactive for some time, for example after 30 minutes without events. Its length therefore varies with user behavior instead of following fixed clock boundaries. A sliding window is different: it groups events that fall within a fixed interval of each other, regardless of gaps in activity. Sessionization is a common requirement in website analytics.

questions.question: Stream joins are commonly classified by whether each input is a stream of activity events or a database changelog. What are the three resulting types?

options.text: Stream-stream, stream-table, and table-table joins
Hash joins, sort-merge joins, and nested-loop joins
Inner joins, left-outer joins, and full-outer joins
Map-side, reduce-side, and broadcast joins

questions.explanation: A stream-stream join matches activity events from two streams within a time window; a stream-table join enriches activity events with a table maintained from a changelog; a table-table join combines two changelogs into a materialized view. Joins on streams are harder than in batch because a new event can arrive at any time, so the processor must keep state. Hash, sort-merge, and nested-loop are join algorithms, inner and outer describe which unmatched rows appear, and map-side and reduce-side are batch implementation strategies; none of them classifies joins by input type.

questions.question: Which scenario is an example of a stream-stream (window) join?

options.text: Joining search and click events by session ID for click-through rates
Enriching each click event with the user's profile from a database changelog
Combining a tweets changelog and a follows changelog into timeline caches
Looking up the tax rate that applied to each sale in a table of tax rates

questions.explanation: Search events and click events are both activity streams, connected by a session ID; to compute click-through rates for each URL, you join them within a window, for example at most one hour apart. Embedding search details in the click event is not equivalent, because you would miss searches with no click. Enriching events with profiles or tax rates is a stream-table join, and combining two changelogs into timelines is a table-table join.

questions.question: In a stream-stream join of search events with click events by session ID, which timing issues must the join handle? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The click may never come if the user abandons their search
Even when it comes, the delay can range from seconds to days or weeks
Due to variable network delays, the click event may arrive before the search event
A click can be joined with a search only if both occur in the same clock minute

questions.explanation: Users abandon searches, return to an old browser tab days later, and networks reorder events, so the join needs a window chosen for the use case (for example one hour), must handle clicks arriving before their search, and must eventually emit searches with no click. Keeping both streams is what lets it measure non-clicks as well as clicks.

optionExplanations.a: A search with no later click is meaningful negative evidence, so the join must eventually expire unmatched search state and report it. Assuming every search gets a click would bias the metric.
optionExplanations.b: Users can click seconds or weeks later, so the correlation window is a product decision rather than a tiny fixed constant. Longer windows require more retained state.
optionExplanations.c: Independent network paths can deliver the click record before the search record even though the search happened first. The join must tolerate out-of-order arrival.
optionExplanations.d: A fixed one-minute boundary would miss legitimate delayed clicks and split pairs that straddle a minute boundary. Correlation should follow session ID and a suitable window.

questions.question: A stream processor joins search events with click events that occur at most one hour apart. What state must it keep?

options.text: The last hour's search and click events, each indexed by session ID
Just a remote database, queried once for every incoming event
The entire history of both streams since the beginning of time
Only click events, since a search with no click carries no information

questions.explanation: The processor keeps the events from the last hour, indexed by session ID. When a search or click arrives, it is added to its index and the other index is checked for an event with the same session ID; if one exists, it emits an event saying which result was clicked. If a search expires without a matching click, it emits an event saying which results were not clicked. The one-hour window bounds the state, so the full history is unnecessary, and unmatched searches are needed for accurate click-through rates.

questions.question: Which scenario is an example of a stream-table join (stream enrichment)?

options.text: Adding user-profile details from a database to each user activity event
Matching two activity event streams with each other within a time window
Joining two database changelogs together into one materialized view
Matching an activity stream with itself to find related events

questions.explanation: In a stream-table join, the input is a stream of activity events containing a user ID, and the output adds profile information about that user from a database; this is called enriching the events. Matching two activity streams, including a stream with itself (a self-join), is a stream-stream join, and joining two changelogs is a table-table join.

questions.question: A stream processor enriches each activity event with user-profile data. How can it avoid a slow remote database query for every event while keeping the profiles current?

options.text: Keep a local copy of the profiles, updated from the database's CDC changelog
Query the remote database for every event, since a local copy cannot stay current
Load a one-time snapshot of the profile database and never update it
Defer the lookups to a nightly batch job and emit the events unenriched

questions.explanation: Querying a remote database per event is slow and risks overloading it. Instead the processor can load a copy of the database locally, as an in-memory hash table or an on-disk index, much like a batch map-side hash join. Unlike a batch job, which uses a point-in-time snapshot, a long-running stream processor must keep the copy current, so it subscribes to the profile database's changelog via change data capture and applies each profile change. A frozen snapshot would go stale, and a nightly job defeats the purpose of streaming.

questions.question: How do the windows in a stream-table join differ from those in a stream-stream join?

options.text: The changelog side's window reaches back to the start of time; the event side may have none
Both sides keep finite windows of equal length, exactly as in a stream-stream join
The activity side keeps an infinite window, while the changelog side keeps a short one
Each side is joined on arrival and discarded, so neither side retains any window of state

questions.explanation: A stream-table join is really a join between two streams, activity events and table changes, so it is very similar to a stream-stream join. The difference is that for the table changelog, the join uses a window reaching back to the 'beginning of time' (conceptually infinite), with newer versions of each record overwriting older ones. For the activity stream, the join might keep no window at all: each event is looked up once and emitted.

questions.question: A stream processor maintains each user's home-timeline cache on a Twitter-like service. Which events must it process to keep the cache correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: When user u sends a new tweet, it is added to the timeline of every user who is following u
When a user deletes a tweet, it is removed from all users' timelines
When u1 follows u2, add u2's recent tweets to u1's cache; when u1 unfollows u2, remove u2's tweets
Following and unfollowing never change an existing timeline cache

questions.explanation: The cached timeline is a materialized join of tweets and follow relationships. New and deleted tweets fan out to followers, while follow and unfollow events add or remove the relevant historical tweets; all four event types must update the view.

optionExplanations.a: A new tweet joins with the posting user's current follower set and is fanned out to each follower's materialized timeline. This is the forward update most people remember.
optionExplanations.b: Deleting a tweet must retract the previously fanned-out entries or the cache stops matching authoritative tweet state. Materialized views need deletion handling as well as insertion.
optionExplanations.c: A follow change alters the join relation itself: following adds relevant recent tweets and unfollowing removes them. Ignoring relationship events leaves cached timelines stale.
optionExplanations.d: Follow and unfollow events change which authors belong in a user's materialized join. Claiming they never affect existing caches overlooks the second input to the join.

questions.question: On a Twitter-like service, a stream processor maintains per-user home-timeline caches from streams of tweets and follow relationships. What is it really maintaining?

options.text: A materialized view over a join of tweets and follows
A full-text search index built over every tweet's words
An aggregation of tweet counts computed over a sliding window
A complex event processing pattern match

questions.explanation: It maintains a materialized view of a query joining two tables, tweets and follows, grouped by follower, roughly: select tweets joined to follows on followee = sender, grouped by follower. The join of the streams corresponds directly to the join of the tables, and the timelines are a cache of the query's result, updated whenever either table changes. A change to tweets joins with the current followers, and a change to follows joins with the current tweets.

questions.question: What do stream-stream, stream-table, and table-table joins all have in common?

options.text: They maintain state from one input and query that state for messages from the other
They join records directly as they arrive, without retaining any earlier input
They require a global order across all inputs, which a partitioned log provides
Only the table-table join among them needs to keep any state at all

questions.explanation: All three keep state built from one join input (recent search and click events, user profiles, or follower lists) and query it for messages from the other input. Because the state changes over time, the order of the events that maintain it matters: following then unfollowing differs from the reverse. A partitioned log preserves order within a partition, but there is usually no ordering guarantee across streams or partitions, which raises the question of which version of the state each event should be joined with.

questions.question: In a stream-table join, a user's profile update and their activity events arrive on different streams with no ordering guarantee between them. What goes wrong?

options.text: It becomes nondeterministic: a rerun may interleave the inputs differently
The join fails outright and reports an ordering error to the operator
The join silently drops the events that arrived near the profile update
The join emits each nearby event twice, once with each profile version

questions.explanation: Which activity events join with the old profile and which with the new depends on how the two streams happen to interleave. If cross-stream order is undetermined, rerunning the same job on the same input may interleave events differently and produce different output. Data warehouses call this a slowly changing dimension and often address it by giving each version of the joined record its own identifier, such as an ID for each tax rate that the invoice references. That makes the join deterministic but rules out log compaction, because every version must be kept.

questions.question: In stream processing, what type of join takes two database changelogs as inputs and emits changes to a materialized view of their join?

options.text: A table-table join
A stream-stream join
A stream-table join
A self-join of one stream

questions.explanation: When both inputs are database changelogs, every change on one side is joined with the latest state of the other side, and the output is a stream of changes to the materialized view of the join, as with tweets and follows producing timelines. Two activity streams make a stream-stream join (a self-join if both are the same stream), and an activity stream plus a changelog makes a stream-table join.

questions.question: Why is fault tolerance relatively easy for batch jobs such as MapReduce?

options.text: Failed tasks rerun on immutable input, and their partial output is discarded
Batch tasks never fail in practice, so no recovery mechanism is needed
Batch jobs checkpoint operator state continuously and restore it, just as Flink does
Every write a batch task makes to HDFS is a distributed transaction

questions.explanation: Input files are immutable, each task writes output to its own file, and output becomes visible only when a task completes successfully, so a failed task can simply be restarted on another machine and its output discarded. The job's output then looks as if every record were processed exactly once, although records may really be processed several times. This is called exactly-once semantics, though effectively-once describes it better.

questions.question: Why can't a stream processor simply use the batch approach of making a task's output visible only once the task has finished?

options.text: A stream is infinite, so a task never finishes processing it
A stream processor produces no output that would need hiding
Stream input is mutable, so a failed task could not be rerun
Streams are already fault-tolerant by construction, so no approach is needed

questions.explanation: Batch fault tolerance relies on a completion point: the output is revealed only after the task succeeds. A stream is unbounded, so processing never finishes and there is no point at which to reveal output. Stream processors instead need finer-grained recovery, such as microbatching, checkpointing, transactions, or idempotent writes. Stream input in a log is in fact immutable and replayable, which is what those techniques build on.

questions.question: Microbatching (as in Spark Streaming) treats a stream as small batches. How large are they typically, and what sets that size?

options.text: About one second, trading scheduling overhead against delay
About one minute, a value dictated by typical network latency
About one millisecond, a value dictated by the CPU clock speed
Exactly one event each, a value chosen by the producer

questions.explanation: Microbatching breaks the stream into small blocks and treats each like a miniature batch job. Batches are typically about one second, a performance compromise: smaller batches incur more scheduling and coordination overhead, while larger ones delay results becoming visible. Microbatching also implicitly gives a tumbling window equal to the batch size, by processing time rather than event time; jobs needing larger windows must carry state over from one microbatch to the next.

questions.question: How does Apache Flink provide fault tolerance for stream operators?

options.text: Rolling checkpoints of operator state written to durable storage
Microbatching with a fixed one-second processing-time window
Synchronous replication of all operator state to three nodes
Nothing beyond restarting the whole job from the first offset of its input

questions.explanation: Flink periodically generates rolling checkpoints of operator state and writes them to durable storage. Checkpoints are triggered by barriers in the message stream, similar to microbatch boundaries but without forcing a particular window size. If an operator crashes, it restarts from its most recent checkpoint and discards any output produced between that checkpoint and the crash, replaying the input from there.

questions.question: Microbatching and checkpointing give exactly-once semantics inside a stream processing framework. Why does that guarantee break down once a job writes to a database, sends to an external broker, or sends emails?

options.text: Output that has left the processor cannot be discarded when a failed task restarts
External output is never retried after a failure, so it can be lost but not duplicated
Database writes are rolled back with the checkpoint, so only emails can repeat
External brokers deduplicate retried messages, so only database writes can repeat

questions.explanation: Inside the framework, the output of a failed microbatch, or anything produced since the last checkpoint, can be discarded and recomputed, so the job behaves as if each input were processed once. Once output leaves the stream processor (a database write, a message to an external broker, an email), the framework can no longer take it back, so restarting the failed task makes that side effect happen twice. Preventing this needs an atomic commit covering outputs, state changes, and input offsets, or idempotent writes. Retries cause duplicates rather than loss, and neither external databases nor external brokers roll back or deduplicate automatically.

questions.question: What must commit atomically for exactly-once processing to appear? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Messages sent downstream, plus the input acknowledgment or consumer-offset advance
Database writes made while processing the event
Changes to the operator's internal state
Only the final output; state and offsets may commit independently

questions.explanation: To appear exactly-once, every output and side effect of processing an event must take effect if and only if processing succeeds: messages to downstream operators or external messaging systems (including email or push notifications), database writes, operator state changes, and the input acknowledgment, including moving the consumer offset. Unlike XA, systems such as Google Cloud Dataflow and VoltDB (with similar features planned for Kafka at the time of writing) keep these transactions internal to the framework, and amortize the overhead by processing several messages per transaction.

optionExplanations.a: Output messages and the input offset must commit together; otherwise a crash can emit output without advancing the offset, or advance it without output, causing duplicates or loss.
optionExplanations.b: Database writes must be in the same atomic unit, or made idempotent another way. A checkpoint alone cannot roll back a database write that was committed independently.
optionExplanations.c: Operator state, such as a window aggregate, must match exactly the input that has been acknowledged. Committing it separately can double-count or skip events after recovery.
optionExplanations.d: Committing only the final output lets state and offsets disagree with that output after a failure. Exactly-once appearance needs all the effects to move together.

questions.question: An idempotent operation has the same effect whether it is performed once or many times. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Setting a key to a fixed value is idempotent; incrementing a counter is not
Incrementing a counter is idempotent; setting a key to a fixed value is not
Both setting a key to a fixed value and incrementing a counter are idempotent
Neither setting a key to a fixed value nor incrementing a counter is idempotent

questions.explanation: Writing a fixed value to a key again simply overwrites it with an identical value, so repeating it changes nothing: idempotent. Repeating an increment adds again, so the counter goes up twice: not idempotent. Idempotence is an alternative to distributed transactions for discarding the effects of failed tasks, because a retried idempotent operation does not take effect twice.

questions.question: A consumer reads messages from Kafka and writes values to an external database. How can that non-idempotent write be made idempotent?

options.text: Store the triggering message's offset with the value to detect replays
Wrap it in a distributed transaction, which is the only possible technique
Retry it until it succeeds, since retrying any write is always harmless
It cannot be made idempotent without changing the database engine

questions.explanation: Every Kafka message has a persistent, monotonically increasing offset. If you store the offset of the message that caused the last write alongside the value, then on replay you can tell whether that update was already applied and skip it. Storm's Trident uses a similar idea. Distributed transactions are another option but not the only one, and blind retries of a non-idempotent write apply it twice.

questions.question: Achieving exactly-once effects through idempotent writes rests on which assumptions? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Retries replay the same messages in the same order
Processing is deterministic
No concurrent writer changes the target; fencing may enforce this
The destination must support two-phase commit

questions.explanation: Idempotence-based recovery assumes that a restarted task replays the same messages in the same order (a log-based broker does this), that processing is deterministic, and that no other node concurrently updates the same value; when failing over between nodes, fencing may be needed to stop a node thought dead that is actually still alive. With those caveats, idempotent operations achieve exactly-once semantics with little overhead and without two-phase commit.

optionExplanations.a: Detecting a repeat, for example by stored offset, works only if the retry replays the same messages in the same order. A log-based broker provides this.
optionExplanations.b: Deterministic processing ensures the same input and prior state produce the same write on retry. Randomness or clock reads during processing would break that.
optionExplanations.c: A concurrent writer could change the value between attempts, so a repeat would act on different state. Fencing a node presumed dead prevents such interference after failover.
optionExplanations.d: Two-phase commit is a separate way to get atomicity and is not a prerequisite. Idempotent writes are usually used precisely to avoid distributed commit.

questions.question: Which state in a stream processor must be recoverable after a failure?

options.text: Windowed aggregations such as counters, and tables or indexes used for joins
Only counters, and only if they are kept in a remote datastore
Nothing needs recovery, since stream state is transient and disposable
Only output messages, since stream operators hold no state of their own

questions.explanation: Any stream process that keeps state, such as windowed aggregations (counters, averages, histograms) and the tables and indexes used for joins, must be able to recover it after a failure. One option is to keep state in a replicated remote datastore, but querying it per message is slow. The alternative is to keep state local to the processor and replicate it periodically, so a replacement task can read the replicated state and resume without data loss.

questions.question: How do Samza and Kafka Streams make local operator state recoverable after a failure?

options.text: They send state changes to a dedicated log-compacted Kafka topic
They periodically write full state snapshots to HDFS
They process every input message redundantly on several nodes
They query a remote database per message instead of keeping state

questions.explanation: Samza and Kafka Streams replicate state changes by sending them to a dedicated Kafka topic with log compaction, much like change data capture; a recovering task rebuilds its local state from that topic. Periodic snapshots to durable storage such as HDFS are Flink's approach, and redundantly processing each input on several nodes is VoltDB's. Querying a remote database per message avoids local state but is slow.

questions.question: When can a stream processor avoid replicating its state at all?

options.text: When replaying the input streams can rebuild it quickly enough
Never; operator state must always be replicated in order to survive
Only when the operator's state happens to be empty at the moment of failure
Only when the job writes no output to any downstream system

questions.explanation: Sometimes state can be rebuilt from the input. If it is an aggregation over a fairly short window, replaying the events for that window may be fast enough; if it is a local replica of a database maintained by CDC, it can be rebuilt from the log-compacted change stream. Which choice is best depends on the infrastructure: in some systems network delay is lower than disk latency and network bandwidth rivals disk bandwidth, so there is no universally ideal trade-off between local and remote state.

questions.question: How does stream processing relate to batch processing?

options.text: It is similar, but runs continuously on unbounded input instead of fixed-size input
It is batch processing with sorting done incrementally over unbounded input
It replaces the filesystem with a relational database as the input source
It is batch processing applied to smaller files that are fixed in size

questions.explanation: In many ways stream processing is like batch processing, but done continuously on unbounded, never-ending streams rather than on fixed-size input. Message brokers and event logs play the role a filesystem plays for batch jobs: producers append records, several jobs consume them independently, and retained input can be replayed. Partitioning, mapping, and joins carry over, while sorting and fault tolerance must change because the input never ends.

questions.question: How does an AMQP/JMS-style message broker assign work, and what is it well suited to?

options.text: It assigns individual messages and deletes them on acknowledgment; it suits task queues
It assigns whole partitions in order to consumers; it suits high-throughput ordered streams
It retains every message for replay; it suits rebuilding derived data systems
It drops messages whenever under load; it suits only approximate metrics

questions.explanation: An AMQP/JMS-style broker assigns individual messages to consumers, which acknowledge each one when processed, and deletes messages once acknowledged. This works as an asynchronous form of RPC, for example a task queue, where the exact order of processing does not matter and nobody needs to reread old messages. Assigning whole partitions and retaining messages for replay describe log-based brokers instead.

questions.question: How does a log-based message broker assign messages and track consumers' progress?

options.text: It assigns each partition to one consumer; consumers checkpoint their offsets
It assigns individual messages and deletes each one when it is acknowledged
It assigns messages by hash to any consumer and records an acknowledgment per message
It broadcasts every message to all consumers and deletes it after a timeout

questions.explanation: A log-based broker assigns all messages in a partition to the same consumer node and always delivers them in the same order; parallelism comes from partitioning. Consumers track progress by checkpointing the offset of the last message processed, and because messages are retained on disk, they can jump back and reread old messages. This resembles database replication logs and log-structured storage engines, and suits stream processors that derive state or output streams from their input.

questions.question: Which of these sources are naturally represented as streams?

options.text: User activity events, sensor readings, and market data feeds
Only message brokers, which generate events on their own
Only databases, since every event originates as a database write
Only sensors, since human activity is too irregular to stream

questions.explanation: User activity events, sensors providing periodic readings, and data feeds such as financial market data are naturally streams. Writes to a database can also be treated as a stream, captured implicitly through change data capture or explicitly through event sourcing; log compaction lets such a stream retain a full copy of the database's contents. A broker transports streams; it does not originate the events.

questions.question: Which purposes of stream processing are commonly distinguished?

options.text: Complex event processing, stream analytics, and maintaining materialized views
Sorting unbounded datasets by key and running sort-merge joins over the sorted output
Only pattern matching, because aggregation requires input that is bounded in size
Only materialized views, because analytics must be done in batch

questions.explanation: Stream processing serves to search for event patterns (complex event processing), compute windowed aggregations (stream analytics), and keep derived data systems up to date (materialized views), with search on streams as a further use. Aggregation works on unbounded input by using windows. Sorting an unbounded dataset makes no sense, so sort-merge joins are not used in stream processing.

questions.question: What does a fault-tolerant stream processor rely on to recover after a failure?

options.text: Replayable input plus checkpoints, snapshots, or logged state
Discarding all output of the failed job and rerunning it, as batch jobs do
Restarting each failed job from the very beginning of its input
Replicating the processing node alone, without any replayable input

questions.explanation: A stream job is long-running and emits output continuously, so it cannot discard all output as a failed batch job does. Recovery instead combines durable, replayable input with saved progress and state: microbatch boundaries, rolling checkpoints, state snapshots, or compacted state-change topics, together with transactions or idempotent writes for outputs. The processor restores a consistent point and reprocesses only the input after it.
